questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A child with generalised oedema, proteinuria of 4 g per day, albumin 1.8 g/dL and normal complement most likely has:
questions.concept: Minimal change disease accounts for most childhood nephrotic syndrome, shows only podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy and responds to corticosteroids without needing a biopsy first.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in a non-diabetic adult in India is:
questions.concept: Its incidence has risen in adults worldwide, it responds poorly to steroids and it recurs in transplanted kidneys, which distinguishes it from minimal change disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Low C3 with normal C4 two weeks after a sore throat in a child with cola-coloured urine indicates:
questions.concept: Alternative pathway activation lowers C3 selectively, and complement normalises within eight weeks, which is a useful confirmatory follow-up test.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Frank haematuria occurring within 1 to 2 days of an upper respiratory infection suggests:
questions.concept: Synpharyngitic haematuria distinguishes IgA nephropathy from the 1 to 3 week latency of post-streptococcal disease, and mesangial IgA deposits confirm it.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane and haemoptysis indicates:
questions.concept: Antibody against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen binds continuously along the membrane, and plasma exchange with cyclophosphamide and steroids is the treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Adult membranous nephropathy is most often associated with antibodies against:
questions.concept: The antibody is present in about 70 percent of primary cases, and its absence should prompt a search for malignancy, hepatitis B or drugs as secondary causes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The principal reason nephrotic patients are hypercoagulable is:
options: Urinary loss of antithrombin III with increased hepatic fibrinogen synthesis
questions.concept: Loss of small anticoagulant proteins in the urine and compensatory hepatic synthesis of large procoagulants together favour thrombosis, classically renal vein thrombosis in membranous nephropathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with hepatitis C, palpable purpura, arthralgia, low C4 and nephritic urine most likely has:
questions.concept: Cryoglobulins activate the classical pathway so C4 falls disproportionately, and treating the hepatitis C with direct-acting antivirals is the primary therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with sensorineural deafness and haematuria in a young man suggests:
questions.concept: X-linked mutations in the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen affect the cochlea, lens and glomerular basement membrane, which shows lamellated splitting on electron microscopy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Under current national guidelines antiretroviral therapy in an HIV-positive adult is started:
options: At diagnosis regardless of CD4 count
Only when an opportunistic infection occurs
questions.concept: The START and TEMPRANO trials showed benefit at every CD4 stratum, and treatment as prevention makes an undetectable viral load non-transmissible.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The preferred first-line antiretroviral regimen for adults in India is:
questions.concept: Dolutegravir has a high genetic barrier to resistance, rapid viral suppression and few interactions, which is why it replaced efavirenz as the anchor drug.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV is started when the CD4 count falls below:
questions.concept: Below 200 the risk of Pneumocystis pneumonia rises sharply, and the same prophylaxis also covers toxoplasmosis and isosporiasis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An HIV patient with CD4 of 40 develops progressive visual loss with perivascular haemorrhages and exudates on fundoscopy. The likely cause is:
questions.concept: The pizza-pie appearance of haemorrhage and necrosis at CD4 below 50 is characteristic, and treatment is ganciclovir or valganciclovir alongside antiretroviral therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia of an HIV patient with CD4 of 80 are most likely due to:
questions.concept: Empirical pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine is given and response assessed at two weeks; a solitary periventricular lesion positive for Epstein-Barr virus DNA favours lymphoma instead.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Paradoxical worsening of tuberculosis a few weeks after starting antiretroviral therapy is called:
questions.concept: Restored immunity mounts an inflammatory response to residual antigen; antiretrovirals are continued and steroids used for severe cases, which is why tuberculosis treatment is started first.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Prevention of mother-to-child transmission is most effective when:
options: Maternal viral suppression is achieved with lifelong antiretroviral therapy
Caesarean section is done in all cases
questions.concept: Transmission risk falls below 2 percent with sustained maternal suppression, which is the basis of the lifelong therapy approach for all pregnant women.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A CD4 count of 150 with dysphagia and white plaques not responding to topical therapy indicates:
questions.concept: Candidiasis extending below the oropharynx is stage 4 disease and warrants systemic fluconazole with initiation of antiretroviral therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Abacavir hypersensitivity is predicted by the presence of:
questions.concept: Screening before prescription has almost eliminated the reaction, which is a systemic multi-organ hypersensitivity that must never be rechallenged.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A plasma NT-proBNP within the normal range in a breathless patient is most useful because it:
options: Effectively excludes heart failure as the cause
questions.concept: The peptide has a high negative predictive value, so a normal level in an untreated patient redirects the diagnosis towards lung disease or anaemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Four drug classes proven to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction are:
options: Beta blocker, renin-angiotensin blocker or ARNI, mineralocorticoid antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor
questions.concept: Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not change survival, whereas the four pillars each independently reduce mortality and should be started early at low dose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the apex with a loud first sound and an opening snap indicates:
questions.concept: A pliable stenosed valve closes forcefully and snaps open, and the shorter the interval from the second sound to the snap the tighter the valve.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An asymptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis and an ejection fraction of 45 percent should be advised:
questions.concept: Left ventricular systolic dysfunction attributable to the valve is a class I indication for intervention even without symptoms, because outcomes deteriorate sharply once the ventricle fails.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The most common cause of mitral stenosis in India remains:
questions.concept: Rheumatic fever remains prevalent, characteristically affects young women and produces commissural fusion amenable to balloon mitral valvotomy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A collapsing pulse with a wide pulse pressure and an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge indicates:
questions.concept: Diastolic runoff into the ventricle lowers diastolic pressure and raises stroke volume, producing the water-hammer pulse and the peripheral signs of Corrigan and de Musset.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Sacubitril-valsartan should not be started within 36 hours of an ACE inhibitor because:
options: Combined neprilysin and ACE inhibition causes bradykinin accumulation and angioedema
questions.concept: Both drugs impair bradykinin degradation, so a washout period is mandatory, and this risk is also why the combination is avoided in patients with prior angioedema.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The blood pressure threshold for stage 1 hypertension by the 2017 ACC/AHA definition is:
questions.concept: The reclassification followed SPRINT, which showed benefit from intensive lowering, although Indian and European guidelines still use 140/90 for the drug-treatment threshold.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Hypertension in a young woman with an abdominal bruit and asymmetric renal size suggests:
options: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery
questions.concept: Fibromuscular dysplasia gives a string-of-beads appearance on angiography in young women, whereas atherosclerotic disease affects older patients with other vascular risk factors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Radiofemoral delay with upper limb hypertension in a young adult indicates:
questions.concept: The obstruction is distal to the left subclavian, so the femoral pulse is delayed and weak, and rib notching from collateral intercostal arteries may be visible on chest radiograph.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension should be evaluated by:
questions.concept: Metanephrines are produced continuously within the tumour so they are more sensitive than catecholamines, which are released episodically and may be normal between attacks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The most appropriate first-line antihypertensive in a 35-year-old with proteinuric chronic kidney disease is:
options: An ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker
questions.concept: Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers intraglomerular pressure and reduces proteinuria, slowing progression beyond the effect of blood pressure lowering alone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In a hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy the mean arterial pressure should be lowered:
options: By no more than 25 percent in the first hour
By 50 percent in the first hour
questions.concept: Chronic hypertension shifts cerebral autoregulation rightward, so precipitous reduction causes watershed cerebral, renal and coronary ischaemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure above target despite:
options: Three drugs at optimal dose including a diuretic
questions.concept: Once adherence and white-coat effect are excluded, the commonest identifiable secondary cause in this group is primary hyperaldosteronism, and spironolactone is the usual fourth agent.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A hypertensive patient with hypokalaemia, low renin and low aldosterone and a family history suggests:
questions.concept: A gain-of-function mutation of the epithelial sodium channel causes sodium retention independent of aldosterone, so it responds to amiloride or triamterene and not to spironolactone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The preferred antihypertensive combination in a hypertensive patient with acute aortic dissection is:
options: Intravenous beta blocker followed by a vasodilator
questions.concept: Reducing the rate of rise of aortic pressure matters as much as the pressure itself, and giving a vasodilator first causes reflex tachycardia that increases shear stress and extends the dissection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF indicates infarction of the:
options: Inferior wall, usually right coronary artery territory
questions.concept: Right coronary occlusion also risks right ventricular infarction and heart block, so right-sided leads should be recorded before nitrates are given.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The preferred reperfusion strategy for ST-elevation myocardial infarction presenting within 12 hours to a PCI-capable centre is:
options: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention within 90 minutes
questions.concept: Primary angioplasty gives better vessel patency, fewer reinfarctions and less intracranial haemorrhage than fibrinolysis when door-to-balloon time can be kept short.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Hypotension after sublingual nitrate in an inferior myocardial infarction should raise suspicion of:
questions.concept: The right ventricle is preload dependent, so venodilatation collapses filling; treatment is fluid loading and avoidance of nitrates and diuretics.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The most specific biomarker for myocardial necrosis is:
questions.concept: Troponins are cardiac-isoform specific and rise within 3 hours and remain elevated for up to two weeks, whereas CK-MB is used mainly to detect reinfarction because it clears faster.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A new pansystolic murmur with acute pulmonary oedema three days after myocardial infarction most likely indicates:
options: Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation
questions.concept: The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply and is vulnerable in inferior infarction; echocardiography confirms it and surgery is urgent.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Persistent ST elevation with a bulging apical impulse six weeks after anterior myocardial infarction indicates:
questions.concept: The thinned scarred wall neither depolarises nor contracts normally, and mural thrombus within the aneurysm is an indication for anticoagulation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Fever, pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial rub two to six weeks after myocardial infarction describes:
questions.concept: It is an autoimmune post-cardiac injury syndrome treated with aspirin or colchicine; other NSAIDs and steroids are avoided early because they impair infarct healing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: The commonest organism causing acute native valve infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users is:
questions.concept: Skin flora inoculated directly into the bloodstream attacks the tricuspid valve, producing right-sided endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: The modified Duke criteria major criteria are:
options: Positive blood cultures with typical organisms and evidence of endocardial involvement
Predisposing heart condition and vascular phenomena
questions.concept: Two major, or one major with three minor, or five minor criteria establish a definite diagnosis, and echocardiography supplies the endocardial evidence.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: The Jones criteria major manifestation that occurs latest after streptococcal infection is:
questions.concept: Chorea may appear months later when other features and even the antistreptolysin titre have resolved, so it is accepted alone as sufficient for the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: Secondary prophylaxis after rheumatic fever with carditis and residual valve disease should continue:
options: For at least 10 years or until age 40, sometimes lifelong
questions.concept: Benzathine penicillin every three weeks prevents recurrent attacks that cause cumulative valve damage, and duration is graded by the presence and severity of carditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: A patient with subacute endocarditis develops painless erythematous macules on the palms and soles. These are:
questions.concept: Janeway lesions are non-tender and embolic, whereas Osler nodes are painful pulp nodules attributed to immune complex deposition.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: Blood cultures in suspected infective endocarditis should be taken as:
options: Three sets from separate sites before antibiotics
One set from a central line
Two sets only after fever settles
questions.concept: Bacteraemia is continuous, so separated sets increase yield and distinguish true infection from contamination, and antibiotics before sampling are the commonest cause of culture-negative disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: Pulsus paradoxus greater than 10 mmHg with muffled heart sounds and raised jugular venous pressure indicates:
questions.concept: Inspiratory ventricular interdependence within a fixed pericardial volume exaggerates the normal inspiratory fall in systolic pressure, and urgent pericardiocentesis is required.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: Prominent x and y descents with a pericardial knock and calcification on chest radiograph indicate:
questions.concept: Rapid early diastolic filling into a rigid pericardium gives a steep y descent and an early third sound, in contrast to tamponade where the y descent is blunted.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever & pericardial disease
questions.stem: Culture-negative endocarditis with a history of contact with farm animals and parturient cats suggests:
questions.concept: Q fever endocarditis is diagnosed serologically by phase I IgG titres and needs prolonged doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine rather than standard regimens.
